sections.text: Page 11 11 FOREWORD Since 1488, we as a navy have provided security at sea and from the sea. We do this with fleet and marine units, supported by all those naval men and women on shore. And we do this with our national and international military and civilian partners. We do this far away and close to home. Since 1488, we have been at the center of history, adapting to new developments and learning from our experiences. By learning from history and the developments within it, we ensure that we remain future-proof, that we can effectively deter and fight to win. It is only logical that we document that history. The result of that logic can be found in this yearbook. I wish you much enjoyment in learning and reading. René P. Tas Vice Admiral (vice-admiraal) Commander of the Naval Forces Foreword Commander of the Naval Forces Vice Admiral R.P. Tas.

Operational Budget The expenditures of the operational budget of CZSK were higher in 2023 than the budget allocated at the beginning of the year (€ 1.034 million) plus additional additions (€ 92 million). Due to personnel shortages, budget was returned for issues elsewhere in the Defense Budget (€ 33 million). As of December 31, 2023, an under-realization of € 0.5 million in the operational budget has been presented. For this, CZSK will receive compensation in 2024. In 2023, the revenues in the operational budget were realized in accordance with the draft budget. Personnel expenditures in 2023 were € 8 million more than included in the draft budget. The cause of this lies primarily with the additional expenditures resulting from the collective labor agreement 2021-2023, against which the personnel shortages stand. Thanks to the Defense Memorandum 2022, CZSK has a higher information budget and more vacancies. Defense Materiel Budget Fund (DMF) In the DMF, expenditures in 2023 were higher than the budget allocated at the beginning of the year (€ 179 million). The budget increased during the year due to additional allocations (€ 84 million) for, among other things, the policy framework for operational stocks (BKI) for main tasks 2 and 3, the effect of higher revenues, and a cash shift from 2024. Due to delays in the realization of, among other things, BKI and projects, the budget (€ 48.3 million) was added to the budgets of 2027 and 2028 through a cash shift. As a result, a surplus of € 21 million was presented as of December 31. The surplus is mainly due to a higher reliability of delivery of goods and services than was estimated at the time of the cash shifts, but also due to higher outsourcing costs than previously budgeted. The budget shifted to 2027 and 2028 will be used for the delayed projects from 2023. Additionally, within the DMF in 2023, € 29.6 million more was received. This includes incidental receipts for, for example, the maintenance of the Portuguese Multipurpose Frigates (M-frigates). Due to the extra efforts in the collection of work for third parties, CZSK has also achieved structurally higher revenues. These additional revenues are and will be used for the maintenance of maritime materiel.

The Directorate Personnel & Organization (P&O) plays a crucial role as a Human Resource (HR) partner in realizing the ambitions of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) regarding personnel readiness and good employment practices. It supports personnel in their development and growth, thereby contributing to career progression within the organization and a positive impact on both Defense and the labor market. By engaging and retaining employees, P&O creates space for flexible deployment in the future and promotes innovative initiatives. All of this aims to provide CZSK with sufficient, well-qualified, and motivated personnel for the execution of its tasks.

Directorate of Personnel and Organization  
For 2023, the focal points of the directorate were: Improving the space for customized agreements, where protocols are guiding but not leading. Further developing opportunities for additional capacity, such as alternative intake and flexible use of labor market potential. Intensifying collaboration with the Personnel Logistics Service Center, the business community, knowledge institutions, the province of North Holland, and employment agencies for the purpose of intake. Further developing, in addition to a stable core of well-trained personnel with long-term contracts, the flexible layer by utilizing different contract forms in an open personnel system. Knowledge building and knowledge safeguarding are anchored through career paths and longer job durations. Further developing a modern innovative learning environment, including simulation and the use of personalized distance learning resources, making it possible to follow training anywhere and anytime. Legal Affairs (JUZA)  
Head: Commander (cdr) (LD) Mr. E.P.J. Schelkers  
The JUZA department is part of the DP&O, one of the four line directorates of CZSK. The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on legal issues that arise. Traditionally, the main areas of law that the department deals with are international law, including the law of the sea, (military) criminal and disciplinary law, and constitutional and administrative law. In addition, JUZA coordinates the handling of complaints within CZSK. Developments  
The CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) was in a difficult situation regarding personnel in 2023. Despite significant salary increases in 2022, particularly for sailors and corporals, the military branch still struggled to find enough new personnel to fill the growing organization. The civilian workforce did increase, which kept the total personnel count nearly stable. In 2023, to combat personnel shortages, the Defense Personnel Plan (DPP) and the Defense Component Personnel Plan (DOPP) were implemented. These aimed to significantly improve the personnel staffing of Defense. The DOPP included measures to increase intake, enhance personnel retention, accelerate career progression, and adjust the operations of CZSK. Some measures from the DOPP included:  
Introduction of the Service Year: on August 21, 2023, the first 12 service year military personnel began the First Maritime Military Training (EMMV). More focus on lateral entry and accelerating career progression. Various programs were developed to make officers and non-commissioned officers deployable more quickly. This includes accelerated programs for the sergeant Network Manager, sergeant Operational Service Operations (ODOPS) Weapon Controller, watch officer, and command center officer (CCO).  
More freedom of choice for future corporals after the corporal training. Implementation of the Marine Technician program, in which a partnership has been established with various Dutch maritime schools. Technical labor market allowance for certain groups of technical personnel.

sections.text: Page 79 79 Operations Directorate Jungle Warfare (Instructor) Course Each year, CLAS and CZSK alternate the organization of jungle training. This year, it was CZSK's turn to organize the jungle training in Suriname in April and May. MTC provided, along with several instructors from the Army, the training cadre for the various courses offered during the jungle training. Survival experts from MTC also supported a training session for NLMARSOF. During the Jungle Movement & Survival Course, the basics of survival and movement in the jungle were taught at an individual level. In the Jungle Warfare Course (JWC), organic units learn to operate and fight in the jungle up to squadron level (SQN level). At the same time, the Jungle Warfare Instructors Course (JWIC) is conducted, which trains cadre members to become instructors. These instructors will form the future continuity of the Corps within the jungle domain. Just like in Norway, the challenging climatic conditions during this training provided the necessary hardship. Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) training in the West In June, MTC once again organized and conducted a two-week SOP training independently in Curaçao as part of relieving the operational units. Six organic sections from the operational units were addressed during this two-week period. The sections were initially coached and then assessed. The training focused on 'find and strike.' sections.text: Page 98 98 Directorate of Operations Zr.Ms. Holland 2023 began for Zr.Ms. Holland with the transfer from OPV-B to OPV-R. OPV-R flew to Curaçao on January 8, 2023, to take over Zr.Ms. Holland from OPV-B. The deployment started with a training period under the leadership of Sea Training Command. The training period was interrupted by a visit from the royal family. On Wednesday, February 1, Zr.Ms. Holland transported King Willem-Alexander, Queen Máxima, and Princess Amalia of Aruba to Curaçao. In Curaçao, the royal family was ceremoniously welcomed before continuing their visit to the Caribbean parts of the kingdom. After the visit from the royal family, the final part of the training was completed, after which Zr.Ms. Holland began its deployment in the Caribbean region. This deployment was not conducted in isolation and was carried out with a shipboard helicopter and a boarding team from the United States Coast Guard. The embarkation of the Fleet Marine Squadron also followed. On May 12, Zr.Ms. Holland returned to Den Helder, after which the crew went on leave. During the leave of OPV-R, OPV-B returned on board Zr.Ms. Holland. There followed several sailing weeks in which exercises were conducted with NLMARSOF (Frogdrill), helicopter qualifications were completed, including operations with the non-maritime helicopter of the police, and the crew ultimately underwent a two-week training period while Zr.Ms. Holland was moored in Cyprus.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.26)
sections.text: Page 99 99 The Operations Directorate carried out activities with Zr.Ms. Tromp in preparation for a subsequent deployment in the Caribbean. Immediately after the leave of OPV-R, Zr.Ms. Holland participated with this crew in Sail and the Marine Days 2023. On June 29, Zr.Ms. Holland served as the flagship of Sail. During the fleet review, the State Secretary of Defense was also on board. The fleet review was conducted together with Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën and Zr.Ms. Tromp. After Sail and the Marine Days, Zr.Ms. Holland underwent major maintenance on the diesel engines until October. On October 2, Zr.Ms. Holland set sail again for sea trials and a port visit in Vlissingen from October 6 to 9. On October 13, OPV-R transferred Zr.Ms. Holland to OPV-W. OPV-W began a Helicopter Qualification (HQ) week at the end of October to qualify helicopter crews. Subsequently, the crew started the Pre-Deployment Training (PDT) in preparation for the planned stationing as SSCG in January 2024. This training was cut short due to escalating tensions in the Middle East following the large-scale attack by Hamas on Israel on October 7. A conflict between Israel and Lebanon was looming, and therefore a Non-combatant Evacuation Operation (NEO) for Dutch citizens in Lebanon and Israel was organized. Zr.Ms. Holland had to depart for Cyprus instead of continuing the PDT to be on standby in case the NEO took place and the Netherlands needed to provide emergency assistance. On November 3, OPV-W was informed that it had to set sail with Zr.Ms. Holland to Cyprus in the context of this Operation Mistral. Preparations for the operation began in Den Helder on November 8, and on November 17, Zr.Ms. Holland sailed to the Mediterranean Sea. During this journey, the crew completed the PDT, including a practice evacuation in Great Britain. On November 28, the ship reached the port city of Limassol in Cyprus. In the first week of December, the crew trained in cooperation with the marines, the FRISC’s, and the NH90 around Cyprus in preparation for the evacuation operation. The units successfully conducted the Full Dress Rehearsal together and were ready to carry out an evacuation in the lower spectrum of violence. Fortunately, this NEO ultimately proved unnecessary, and the operational deployment was limited to exercises with Italian, British, and American units and reconnaissance flights with the helicopter.

Shortly after the Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) was alerted to participate in a French exercise in New Caledonia, the security situation in Khartoum deteriorated. The fighting between the government army and militias intensified to such an extent that the evacuation of compatriots became necessary. The MSTU was tasked with conducting the evacuation together with units from the Royal Netherlands Air Force, personnel from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Brigade Speciale Beveiligingsopdrachten (KMAR). Non-combatant Evacuation Operation (NEO) Sudan In April, 1MCG prepared for an activation exercise in New Caledonia. Shortly before the start, on April 18, the news came that the situation in Sudan had deteriorated to such an extent that a Non-combatant Evacuation Operation (NEO) was necessary to evacuate Dutch citizens from the area. The following day, 1MCG flew together with the Brigade Special Security Assignments (BSB) of the Military Police to Jordan, from where the operation was directed. Here, the unit became acquainted with the Rapid Consular Support Team (SCOT) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (BuZa) and awaited the green light for departure to Sudan. In the evening of April 22, news arrived that partner countries near Khartoum had taken control of an airport, allowing the operation to commence.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.37)
sections.text: Page 110 110 Operations Directorate Two aircraft from the Royal Netherlands Air Force flew from Jordan to Sudan. The first aircraft was filled with 60 personnel, consisting of the advance party of marines, the SCOT, and the BSB. The second contained only six marines and was intended to, if possible, maximize the evacuation capacity. The Sudanese army did not grant permission for the first aircraft to land due to the overcrowding of the airport by foreign military personnel. The second aircraft arrived later and was allowed to land. Despite the very limited crew, the first evacuation flight could take place within an hour, transporting several dozen civilians. After this, the first aircraft was also able to land, and a total of seven more evacuation flights followed. When the British took over the airport from the Germans and the Netherlands would no longer conduct flights, the leadership, in consultation with the British, decided to leave four marines at the airport from April 26 to April 29. They worked together with the Royal Marines in Sudan during the Non-combatant Evacuation Operation.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.38)
sections.text: Page 111 111 Directorate of Operations Marine Commandos remained available to provide assistance in 'complicated cases': Dutch nationals with an expired passport or families where only part had a Dutch passport. The remaining marines operated independently on-site but remained in contact with the SCOT, which continued to operate from Jordan and was responsible for screening evacuees. As a result, the evacuation of dozens of Dutch citizens was made possible. In total, at least 160 Dutch nationals were evacuated from Sudan, more than 85 of whom were transported by the Air Force's aircraft. Other Dutch nationals were able to fly on flights from other European countries. On the Dutch flights, approximately 130 evacuees from 18 other nationalities were also taken. Functional Training June and July were focused on functional training for both 1MCG and 2MCG, namely the Sierra Team Commanders Course (STCC) and the Designated Marksman Course (DMC). Both courses began in the Netherlands, with the continuation taking place in Otterburn (UK). During the STCC, the corporals from the Raiding Squadrons learned to lead a Sierra team (S-team), focusing on the handling of group weapons, and learned to operate as an S-Team. In the first week, the teams received training in the use of all weapon systems: FN MAG, .50 QCB, and 60mm mortars. In the second week, the teams prepared for the final phase in Otterburn by practicing equipment camouflage and going through scenarios with blank ammunition. In Otterburn, the S-teams underwent Live Fire Training. A new element was the S-team competition, where the S-teams competed against each other with challenges in estimating distances, shooting, positioning, and gun drills, with the best-performing team receiving the trophy. To conclude the training, the units practiced providing fire support under the direction of the Troop Commander (TC). The Designated Marksman Course emphasized precision skills. During the training, participants learned to deal with ballistics, wind influences, breathing techniques, and aiming devices. They practiced identifying targets, taking positions, and shooting quickly and accurately with the HK417. During the first phase in the Netherlands, the shooters practiced their basic skills by firing at paper targets, first at 100 meters and ultimately at 600 meters. They then trained in shooting at moving targets and delivering fire in dynamic situations. In Otterburn, participants were able to train under varying weather conditions and

sections.text: Page 160 160 Directorate of Material Maintenance Navigation and Training Bridge The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for practicing all navigation procedures and safe mooring and unmooring. Deployment The Van Kinsbergen sails approximately 200 days per year. The main user is the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The vessel serves as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development. Besides the KIM, the Netherlands-Belgium Operational School (NL-BEOPS) is also a major user. Students at NLBEOPS receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of Non-Commissioned Officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the agreement, the MIWB has the vessel available for a number of weeks for training purposes. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical voyages on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder. These include subjects such as loading technology and maritime law. Within the agreement, there is an exploration of how this collaboration can be expanded to further modernize and improve education within both institutions. The highest quality is pursued in order to train future-proof nautical professionals ready for the maritime labor market.

sections.text: Page 168 168 Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Vision In September, CZMCARIB redefined its mission in line with its main task, mission, and environmental factors, and articulated it more clearly. Previously, this was: "CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean." The new vision states: "CZMCARIB, as a reliable security partner, protects the Caribbean part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and contributes to stability in the Caribbean with adaptive military (continuation) capability and a robust information position." The vision emphasizes the adaptive military capability of CZMCARIB, which is crucial for responding quickly and effectively to threats and hostilities, thereby maintaining the integrity and interests of the Caribbean part of the Kingdom in the region. This formulation also underscores the importance of a robust information position, which is of critical significance in executing the second main task of CZMCARIB. A strong information position enables the organization to respond effectively to threats such as drug trafficking, but is also important in promoting international cooperation. Finally, the importance of partnerships and the necessity of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan transporting soldiers from the Company in the West to Bonaire is highlighted.

Bröker MSec Commander of the Patrol Area Caribbean: A.D. Berkhout The Mission Statement of the Defense Security and Protection Organization is: ‘We ensure the physical security of the interests of the Defense components, day and night. The core values associated with this are cooperation, professionalism, reliability, communication, and responsibility.’ Access Control (AC) The DBBO carries out access control based on the Access Regulation A/007 of the Defense Security Policy (DBB). Daily checks are conducted on behalf of the garrison commanders. The access controls also include inspections. Access controls are carried out in cooperation with colleagues from the Curaçao and Aruba military (CURMIL and ARUMIL). Patrol, Intervention, and First Response Tasks The patrol, intervention, and First Response tasks that the DBBO carries out together with colleagues from ARUMIL and CURMIL are tasks that are performed every day throughout the year. The specifics arising from these tasks are shared with the garrison leadership to promote security awareness among everyone. Training, Certification, and Education The regular Integrated Professional Skills Training (IBT) applies to the DBBO as well as to ARUMIL and CURMIL. In blocks of 6 weeks, personnel are kept competent and capable by the IBT trainers according to the standards of the National Act. Additionally, the IBT trainer supports the Security and Protection (B&B) training of CURMIL and ARUMIL. Personnel In mid-2023, the DBBO commenced security operations at Coast Guard Support Point (KWSP) Hato and MSK Savaneta. At Hato, the organization carries this out in cooperation with an employee from Securitas (for Coast Guard (KW) tasks). At MSK Savaneta, colleagues from ARUMIL provide support. In addition to these additions to the DBBO personnel, a number of regular personnel changes took place.

On Thursday, January 11, the traditional New Year's reception was held, hosted by the commandant of KIM and the dean of the Faculty of Military Sciences. The New Year's reception took place in 't Zaaltje of the Corps of Cadets. Annually, the cadets receive an invitation to the Wiener Ball. On February 11, this could take place for the 53rd edition after the coronavirus pandemic, where three couples from the Corps of Cadets participated. In the weekends leading up to the ball, mandatory participation in the rehearsals took place. In mid-April, a week of vocational education was scheduled, the so-called BO week. During this week, the mandatory KIM cross for the cadets took place, the boxing gala, and for the first time, a symposium on the Sugar Festival. This year's BO week concluded with the Dies Natalis, themed 'Challenges at Sea'. sections.text: Page 198 198 Appendices The evening before the grand commissioning, the now traditional MARKAP concert took place. The concert was held outdoors and is intended for the parents of the cadets, the permanent staff of the Royal Naval College (KIM), and employees of the KIM location and their partners. On Friday, June 23, the grand commissioning took place, during which a total of 84 young officers took the oath or made a promise. Subsequently, in the afternoon, the officer diplomas were awarded. After nearly a year of intensive training, the marines were 'welcomed' by their parents, the Commander of the Marine Corps (CKM), and the Commander of the Netherlands Defence Academy (C-NLDA) at the beginning of July. This part of the training has prepared the candidates for their first role as Troop Commander (TC) in operational marine units. The first role is essentially a hands-on position. The Practical Training for Officer of Marines (POTOM) reflects this by dedicating most of the training time to practical situations, focusing on the knowledge, skills, and attitudinal aspects that the candidate immediately needs in the role of a warrior (in accordance with the Training Vision of the Royal Institute for the Navy 2017-2030, established by C-KIM, dated April 7, 2017). On October 6, the installation of the 2023 promotion took place in the presence of their family members and those who were installed 50 years ago, the 1973 promotion. Unfortunately, the entrance of the banner group occurred during the grand commissioning.

Coast Guard Netherlands Director: Captain (ktz) N.I.J. Kuipers EMSD The global security situation has drawn significant attention in 2023 to Dutch interests in the North Sea, the primary operational area of the Coast Guard. The awareness of the vulnerability of vital infrastructure at sea was underscored in 2023 by the presence of Russian research vessels in the North Sea. Although the Coast Guard does not yet have a formal task in this aspect of Maritime Security, it contributed to situational awareness at sea, an important condition for adequate protection of vital Dutch interests. The Maritime Information Node (MIK) provided an increasing contribution from its information position to the security picture for Dutch shipping and to the enforcement of sanctions against the Russian Federation. The ‘Bulletin maritime sanctions Russia’ has proven to be of great added value for the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, ports, Customs, and the Inspectorate for the Environment and Transport (ILT). The MIK is an example of successful cooperation as it occurs within the Coast Guard organization with various services and partners. The analytical function of the Coast Guard will be further developed in the coming years. In terms of service delivery, the Coast Guard has carried out its tasks in the North Sea as assigned. sections.text: Page 201 201 Appendices The availability of enforcement vessels at sea was lower than required for effective task execution. In consultation with the enforcement services and the Rijksrederij, the Coast Guard was able to deploy the emergency tug Guardian to fill some gaps in the sailing schedule. On the advice of the State Advocate, the planned assignment of ship crews from the Rijksrederij could not proceed, which meant that the patrol vessels Visarend and Zeearend were not deployable outside of the planned services. The additional sailing capacity for enforcement promised in 2023 is an absolute requirement to make a step towards 24/7 execution of this primary task at sea. In June 2023, the tender for the construction of the new Maritime Operations Center (MOC) and the Diversion, Testing, and Training Center (UTT) was put on the market, marking an important step in the realization of a new and modern Coast Guard center. This will have a positive effect on the operations of the Coast Guard. The preliminary award of the contract for the new construction has already taken place. Its delivery is scheduled for 2026. At the beginning of 2023, the Coast Guard did not implement the new incident management application, Guardion Coastguard, as planned. In particular, the market product purchased for incident registration, in accordance with the advice of the ICT Assessment Bureau, proved to have limitations regarding its usability in the operational center. The project replaced this component with a solution that is integrated into Guardion Coastguard, developed by JIVC Maritime IT. The Coast Guard reviewed its organization and mapped out the necessary personnel capacity that aligns with the assignments and ambitions of the clients from 2025. The required personnel capacity has been summarized in the Council for the Coast Guard in the so-called imbalance note. This also includes other necessary capacities, such as investments in personnel and ships to carry out 24/7 enforcement tasks and investments in personnel and systems for the execution of tasks in the field of Maritime Security, Enforcement, and Services. The Council definitively approved the resolution of this imbalance in June 2023 and allocated the necessary financial resources for this purpose. This allows the reorganization process to begin.
